column2: On the authority of Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him), from the Prophet (Allah the Exalted bless him and his family and grant them peace), in what he relates from his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, that He said: “O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and have made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another. O My servants,

all of you are astray except those I have guided, so seek guidance from Me and I will guide you. O My servants, all of you are hungry except those I have fed, so seek food from Me and I will feed you. O My servants, all of you are naked except those I have clothed, so seek clothing from Me and I will clothe you. O My servants, you err by night and by day, and I forgive all sins, so seek My forgiveness and I will forgive you.

O My servants, you will never attain the power to harm Me so as to harm Me, nor attain the power to benefit Me so as to benefit Me. O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were as pious as the most pious heart of any one man among you, that would not increase My dominion in anything.
O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were as wicked as the most wicked heart of any one man among you, that would not decrease My dominion in anything.

O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were to stand together on one plain and ask of Me, and I gave each one what he asked, that would not decrease what I have except as much as a needle decreases [the sea] when it is dipped into the sea.

O My servants, it is only your deeds that I record for you and then repay you for in full. So whoever finds good, let him praise Allah; and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself.” Reported by Muslim.
Ḥarramtu (“I have forbidden”): I have prohibited.
Al-ẓulm (“injustice”): linguistically, putting a thing in other than its proper place.

“For Myself”: out of My favour, generosity and kindness to My servants; so I do not punish the innocent for bad deeds he did not do, nor punish anyone for another's sin, nor reduce the doer of good anything of the reward of his good deeds, nor judge between people except with justice and equity.
“And have made it forbidden among you”: I have ruled that it is forbidden to you.
Fa-lā taẓālamū (“so do not wrong one another”): with the ẓāʾ doubled or light; its root is tataẓālamū. Let none of you wrong another.
“All of you are astray”: from the truth, if left [to yourselves] and to what your nature calls for of ease and neglect of the Sharīʿah,
“except those I have guided”: whom I have enabled to carry out the command and avoid the prohibition.
“So seek guidance from Me”: ask Me to show you the path of truth and to bring you to it,
“and I will guide you”: I will set up clear proofs of it for you and enable you to follow them.
“So seek food from Me”: ask Me for food.
Tukhṭiʾūna (“you err”): with ḍammah on the tāʾ according to the well-known narration; it is also narrated with fatḥah on it and on the ṭāʾ (takhṭaʾūna): you commit sins.
“And I forgive all sins”: except shirk and whatever He does not will to forgive.
“So seek My forgiveness”: ask Me for forgiveness, which is the covering of the sin, the erasing of its trace and safety from its consequence.
“Stand together on one plain”: in one land and one place.
Al-mikhyaṭ (“a needle”): with kasrah on the mīm, sukūn on the dotted khāʾ and fatḥah on the yāʾ; the needle.
Uḥṣīhā (“I record”): I register them precisely and preserve them by My knowledge and My angels.
“Then repay you for in full”: I give you their recompense, full and complete.
“So whoever finds good”: reward and bliss, through having been enabled to follow their causes,
or a good and pleasant life,
“let him praise Allah”: for enabling him to do the acts of obedience that brought about that good and reward, out of His favour and mercy.
Ghayra dhālik (“otherwise”): evil.
“Let him blame no one but himself”: for his soul preferred its desires to the pleasure of its Provider, was ungrateful for His blessings and did not submit to His rulings.

The prohibition of injustice, which is agreed upon in every religion, since all religions agree on preserving life, lineage, honour, intellect and wealth, and injustice occurs in these or some of them. The greatest injustice is shirk; the Exalted said: “Indeed, shirk is a great injustice” [Luqmān 31:13].
The obligation to turn to the Master in everything that befalls a person, because all creation needs Him and is unable to bring about its benefits or ward off its harms except by His making it easy.

So He must be singled out in all kinds of worship—asking, humble entreaty, seeking help and the rest—for He alone creates the servant, guides him, provides for him, gives him life and death, and forgives his sins.
The perfection of His justice, the Exalted, in His being free of injustice; and the perfection of His dominion, which is not increased by obedience nor decreased by sins;
and the perfection of His freedom from need, for His treasuries are not exhausted or decreased by giving;

and the perfection of His kindness to His servants, for He loves them to ask Him for all their religious and worldly interests, just as they ask Him for guidance and forgiveness. To Him, the Exalted, belongs absolute perfection in His essence, His attributes and His actions.
The printed text reads كمال فعله and يجب; the context indicates كمال عدله (“the perfection of His justice”) and يحب (“He loves”), which the translation follows.
The origin of piety and wickedness is the hearts: when the heart is righteous and pious, the limbs are righteous, and when the heart is wicked, the limbs are wicked.
All good is from Allah the Exalted's favour to His servants, without their deserving it,
and all evil is from the son of Ādam himself, through following the whims of his soul.
